lessons.title: Breeding goals and breeding systems
lessons.html:
Start with a breeding goal

A breeding system is the plan for which animals are mated to which, when and why. Before choosing a system, decide what the farm needs to sell. A weaner calf producer wants fertile cows that wean heavy calves on veld. A dairy wants high milk solids and good udders. A wool farmer wants fine, heavy fleeces from Merinos; a mutton farmer may choose Dorpers or Meatmasters for growth and hardiness.

Main breeding systems

SystemWhat it isWhen used
Pure breedingMating animals of the same breedStud herds, keeping breed traits
CrossbreedingMating two or more breedsCommercial herds wanting hybrid vigour
Terminal crossCrossbred offspring all sold, none keptLamb and weaner production
Rotational crossSires of different breeds used in turnKeeping hybrid vigour in replacement females
CompositeA stable mix of breeds bred like a pure breedSimpler management with some hybrid vigour

Hybrid vigour

Crossbred animals often perform better than the average of their parents, especially in fertility, survival and hardiness. This is called hybrid vigour or heterosis. For example, a Nguni or Afrikaner cow crossed with a Simmentaler or Angus bull may wean a heavier calf while the cow stays adapted to local conditions.

Avoid inbreeding

Mating closely related animals, such as a bull with his daughters, increases the risk of weak calves, low fertility and defects. Change bulls or rams before their daughters are bred, and keep records of parentage.

lessons.title: Selecting breeding animals
lessons.html:
Choosing sires and dams

Selection is how genetic progress is made. The sire has the biggest effect because he mates many females, so choose him carefully.

What to look at

  • Fertility – females that calve or lamb regularly; bulls and rams that pass a breeding soundness examination by a vet, including the testes and semen.
  • Performance records – weaning weights, growth, milk yield, fleece weight. Stud animals may have estimated breeding values (EBVs) from breed societies.
  • Conformation – sound legs and feet, good teeth, correct udder, no defects.
  • Adaptation – tick and heat tolerance for the area.
  • Temperament – calm animals are safer and easier to manage.

Culling

Remove animals that do not meet the goal: open or late-calving females, poor mothers, animals with bad udders, feet or teeth, and those with weak progeny. Culling is as important as selection, because it removes poor genes and frees grazing for productive animals.

Replacement heifers and ewes

Keep replacements from your best-performing mothers. Grow heifers well so they reach the target mating weight for their breed; heifers mated too light often struggle to calve and to conceive again.

Safety with bulls and rams

Bulls, especially dairy bulls, are dangerous. Never enter a camp or pen alone with a bull, always have an escape route, and handle him in a strong crush. Rams also butt and can injure people.

lessons.title: Running and maintaining the breeding season
lessons.html:
Planning the breeding season

A defined breeding season gives a short, predictable calving or lambing season. In summer rainfall areas, many beef farmers mate cows so that calves are born when the veld is green and cows can recover. Choose dates that match the feed supply on your farm.

Before the season

  1. Have bulls and rams examined by a vet for breeding soundness about a month or two before mating.
  2. Check body condition of females; thin females conceive poorly. Supplement if needed.
  3. Complete vaccinations on the health calendar before mating, as your vet advises.
  4. Decide the mating ratio of females per sire suitable for the camp size and sire age.
  5. Allocate groups and record which sire goes into which camp.

During the season

Watch the sires: check they are working, not lame and not injured. A bull that is injured during the season can leave many cows open. Keep good water and grazing in breeding camps.

After the season

Remove sires on the planned date. Have females pregnancy tested by a vet and decide what to do with open females. Record calving or lambing dates, birth weights, problems at birth and weaning weights. Use these records to judge sires and dams and to plan next season.

Measuring success

Track the calving or lambing percentage, the length of the calving season and the weaning weight per female mated. If results drop, look at nutrition, sire fertility and disease.

Key points

  • Set a clear breeding goal before choosing a breeding system.
  • Crossbreeding gives hybrid vigour; avoid inbreeding by changing sires.
  • Select on fertility, records, conformation and adaptation, and cull firmly.
  • Have sires checked for breeding soundness before each season.
  • Use a defined season and good records to measure and improve results.

All are sold and none are kept for breeding
